content: 1. For critically ill children, prioritize feeding every 2 hours, while aiming for at least every 3 hours initially for others. Night feeds are essential, and staff schedules may need adjustment to ensure this. If all night feeds cannot be provided, space them evenly to avoid prolonged fasting, which increases the risk of hypoglycemia and mortality. 2. Engage mothers and caregivers in feeding by demonstrating proper techniques and supervising them. If a child’s intake does not reach 80 kcal/kg/day despite frequent feeds, coaxing, and re-offering, administer the remaining feed via a nasogastric tube. Do not exceed 100 kcal/kg/day during the initial phase. 3. In hot climates, provide additional water to children, as the feeds may not contain sufficient water to compensate for sweating. 4. During the catch-up growth phase, most children can be managed as outpatients. Transition gradually from starter formula F-75 to catch-up formula F-100 or ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) over 2–3 days as tolerated. 5. Replace F-75 with an equal amount of F-100 for 2 days. On the third day, increase each feed by 10 ml until some feed remains uneaten, which typically occurs at an intake of about 200 ml/kg/day. After transitioning, provide frequent feeds in unlimited amounts, targeting 150–220 kcal/kg/day and 4–6 g of protein/kg/day. 6. If using RUTF, start with small, regular meals and encourage the child to eat often (initially 8 meals/day, later 5–6 meals/day). If the child cannot consume the full RUTF amount during the transition phase, supplement with F-75 until they can eat a full RUTF meal. If the child cannot take at least half the recommended RUTF amount in 12 hours, stop RUTF and revert to F-75, reintroducing RUTF after 1–2 days. 7. For breastfeeding children, offer breast milk before every RUTF feed. After the transition phase, refer the child to outpatient care or a community feeding program for rehabilitation. 8. Ensure proper hygiene during feeding by washing hands, sitting with the child on the lap, and gently offering feeds. Encourage the child to eat without force-feeding and provide clean water in a cup during RUTF consumption. 9. Monitor for early signs of congestive heart failure, such as rapid pulse, fast breathing, basal lung crepitations, enlarged liver, gallop heart rhythm, or raised jugular venous pressure. If pulse and breathing rates increase (breathing by 5 breaths/min and pulse by 25 beats/min) over two consecutive 4-hour readings, reduce feed volume to 100 ml/kg/day for 24 hours, then gradually increase as tolerated. 10. Assess progress by monitoring weight gain daily before feeding and calculating weight gain every 3 days as g/kg/day. Poor weight gain (<5 g/kg/day) requires full reassessment, moderate gain (5–10 g/kg/day) necessitates checking intake targets and infection status, and good gain (>10 g/kg/day) indicates recovery. 11. For infants under 6 months with severe acute malnutrition, consider organic causes and treat appropriately. Admit infants with complicating factors such as general danger signs, recent weight loss, ineffective breastfeeding, bilateral pitting edema, or adverse social circumstances for inpatient care. 12. Re-establish effective exclusive breastfeeding by the mother or caregiver. If not possible, provide commercial infant formula with guidance on safe preparation and use. For infants with edema, supplement breastfeeding with infant formula, F-75, or diluted F-100. For non-edematous infants, prioritize expressed breast milk, followed by commercial formula, F-75, or diluted F-100. 13. During nutritional rehabilitation, adhere to principles for older children but account for young infants’ reduced ability to excrete salt and urea, especially in hot climates. Assess the physical and mental health of mothers or caregivers and provide necessary support. 14. Before discharge, ensure the infant’s vaccination status and routine interventions are up to date. Link mothers or caregivers with community follow-up and support services. Discharge from nutritional care only when the child is breastfeeding effectively or feeding well with replacement feeds, has adequate weight gain, and achieves a weight-for-length equal to or higher than -2 z-scores. 15. For children with eye signs of vitamin A deficiency, administer vitamin A orally on days 1, 2, and 14. If corneal clouding or ulceration is present, provide additional care to prevent corneal rupture, including chloramphenicol or tetracycline eye drops, atropine eye drops, and saline-soaked eye pads. 16. For severe anemia, perform a blood transfusion only if hemoglobin (Hb) is <4 g/dl or 4–6 g/dl with respiratory distress. Administer whole blood at 10 ml/kg slowly over 3 hours, with furosemide at 1 mg/kg IV at the start. Monitor for signs of heart failure and adjust transfusion speed or stop if necessary. 17. For skin lesions in kwashiorkor, zinc supplementation is essential. Apply barrier creams to raw areas and gentian violet or nystatin cream to sores. 18. For continuing diarrhea, treat giardiasis with metronidazole if stool microscopy is unavailable or clinical suspicion exists. Diagnose lactose intolerance only if watery diarrhea occurs promptly after milk-based feeds and resolves when milk is reduced or stopped. Use low-lactose feeds like F-75 or alternatives in exceptional cases. 19. For osmotic diarrhea, use cereal-based starter F-75 or commercially available isotonic F-75. Gradually introduce catch-up F-100 or RUTF. 20. If tuberculosis is suspected, perform a Mantoux test and chest X-ray if possible. Children admitted with complicated severe acute malnutrition can be transferred to outpatient care during the rehabilitation phase once medical complications are resolved, appetite is restored, and edema is reduced. 21. Discharge children from nutritional treatment programs only when their weight-for-height/length is ≥-2 z-scores or mid-upper-arm circumference is ≥125 mm, with no edema for at least 2 weeks. Ensure frequent meals with high energy and protein content, and counsel mothers on appropriate feeding practices. 22. Plan follow-up for discharged children until full recovery, coordinating with outpatient departments, nutrition rehabilitation centers, or local health workers for continued supervision.
